job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Erik Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at my desk by 8:30 in the back office of a regional bank, in the loan processing team. I started in September after my finance degree. I check mortgage and car-loan applications for missing documents, enter the numbers and send them to an underwriter. I eat lunch with two colleagues, Priya and Dennis. I share a flat with my brother Emre, who's a warehouse worker, and we split the rent and argue about the thermostat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's another tool, like email was. A few things get quicker, a few mistakes get caught earlier, and the bank carries on. I'd tell Emre there's no need to be dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay on the AI side. My real worry is money: after my loan payment and rent I've got almost nothing, and a trainee-level grade doesn't pay a lot. If the bank has a bad year, back-office staff get cut. That would happen with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well. I'd use the AI helper the bank approved for drafting emails, because everybody does a bit. I'd also try to move to the underwriting side within two years, since that's where the better pay is. I'd pay my loan on time and keep about 50 a month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A low hum of money worry, but I'm used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move to underwriting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year of clean work and a good word from my manager, Ms Okafor. Underwriters decide and take the responsibility, so there's some job security, and the pay is about a third higher. It's what I'd aim for either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your brother see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emre thinks I worry too much. His warehouse is already using scanners and machines to count stock and he says nobody has been fired yet. We both pay the rent, and if either of us lost a job it would be bad for both.

say: It's another tool, like email was, so no need to be **dramatic**.
A few things get quicker and a few mistakes get **caught earlier**.
think: My real worry is **money**, with almost nothing left after the loan and rent.
If the bank has a bad year, **back-office staff** get cut, AI or not.
do: Do the job well and use the bank-approved **AI helper** for emails.
Aim to move to **underwriting** within two years and save 50 a month.
feel: **Calm enough**, with a low hum of money worry.
S0.quote: A few things get quicker, a few mistakes get caught earlier, and the bank carries on.
fieldNote: Pragmatic and steady: sees AI as one more **tool**.
Shares rent with his brother **Emre**, so one job loss would hit both.
Real concern is the **bank's finances** and pay, not AI.

steps.text: Use the bank-approved AI helper to draft routine emails
Ask Ms Okafor about moving to the underwriting team next year
Save 50 a month on top of the loan payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the job, but a bank can't just flip a switch. There are rules and checks. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools while the bank is still training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the work I do, checking documents and entering numbers, is the first thing the software does. Priya and I have already seen the document scanner make our team smaller by one. The bank says it's natural turnover. I'm junior, and I think about that every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new document system fast, because the team that knows it will be kept. I'd ask for a place on the underwriting course and do it on my own time if needed. I'd quietly put my CV on two job sites, just so it's out there. I'd put aside whatever I can, aiming at three months of costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense. I'm not panicking, but I notice I'm checking the news about the bank's results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the team got smaller by one. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guy called Tomasz left in the summer, and they didn't replace him. The work spread across the rest of us. Nobody said anything in a meeting, it just happened. That's how I think it will go: quietly, one person at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your name came up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask what it would take to move into another team, and if not, take a payoff and look elsewhere. I'd feel bitter, but I wouldn't make a scene. I'd rather leave on good terms, because the industry is small.

say: The job will change, but a bank can't **flip a switch**, because of rules and checks.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools while the bank is **still training**.
think: Document checking and number entry are the **first** things software takes.
Our team already shrank by one, and as the junior I **think about it weekly**.
do: Learn the **new document system** fast and ask for the underwriting course.
Put my CV on **two job sites** and aim for three months of costs.
feel: A bit **tense**, checking the news about the bank's results.
S1.quote: Nobody said anything in a meeting, it just happened. That's how I think it will go: quietly, one person at a time.
fieldNote: Observes cuts as **quiet attrition**, which fits his measured outlook.
Would leave **on good terms** rather than make a scene.
Mood is anxious because his own role is **plainly exposed**.

steps.text: Learn the bank's new document scanning system in the first month
Do the underwriting course on weekends if the bank won't pay
Post my CV on two job sites and answer recruiters
Build three months of rent and loan costs in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle. I'd talk about transition support and say the government should have plans. But I'd be careful, because nobody wants to be the junior who says the bank is going to be cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my guess is that I'd have eighteen months at most. A loan processor with a finance degree is high on the list. The bank would say 'redeploy', but I'd bet on cuts. I have no savings, and my brother has a warehouse job that might outlast mine by about three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my money into a boring savings account and cut costs hard: no takeaways, no new phone, cancel the gym. I'd start applying for hands-on jobs now, like in logistics or the energy sector, anywhere that needs people on site. I'd also see if Emre's warehouse is hiring, even though that's not my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick feeling. I'd be doing sums at 2 a.m. and getting the same answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Emre's warehouse might outlast your job. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strange, because I'm the one with the degree. We grew up being told that studying meant safety. Now I'm thinking I might be asking my brother for a favour. I would, though. Family is family, even if I'd be embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, then my phone plan, then I'd talk to the landlord. The loan I'd keep paying as long as I can, because defaulting follows you around. I'd rather eat rice.

say: It's **too fast** for anyone to handle, and government needs transition plans.
I'd stay **careful** at work, because nobody wants to be the junior predicting cuts.
think: I'd have about **eighteen months** at most as a loan processor.
The bank would say 'redeploy', but I'd bet on **cuts**.
do: Cut costs hard and move savings into a **boring account**.
Apply for **hands-on jobs** in logistics and energy, and check Emre's warehouse.
feel: A **sick feeling**, doing sums at 2 a.m. with the same answer.
S2.quote: We grew up being told that studying meant safety. Now I'm thinking I might be asking my brother for a favour.
fieldNote: Expects job loss within two years and has **no savings**, so alarmed.
Notes the irony that his **brother's** warehouse job may outlast his degree.
Still prioritises the **loan** because default follows people around.

steps.text: Cancel the gym, takeaways and the phone upgrade
Move my savings into a plain savings account
Apply for logistics and energy company site jobs
Ask my brother Emre about openings at his warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it gives us time, but I'd want governments to start now with training funds. I'd tell friends that banking jobs will look different by 2031 and to pick up some skill that's more than processing paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's what I'd call a ticking clock I can work with. I'd be 27, with a promotion hopefully, and I'd have paid off a decent bit of my loan. The risk is that I stay in the back office and do the same thing for four years. That's the version of me that gets caught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to underwriting or customer advice in the first two years, get a recognised qualification, and learn every tool the bank brings in. I'd also look at moving to a smaller firm where I'd do many jobs, not one. I'd save 100 a month and pay the loan down aggressively.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast. You buy a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a smaller firm give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Variety. In the big bank I'm one of eighty people doing one step. In a small firm I'd see the whole process and be harder to replace. The pay is lower, but I'd learn more. I'd take that trade at 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay put?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A promotion with real money. Or the bank saying clearly what happens to staff. If it's vague I'd go. If they put a plan in writing I might stay.

say: It gives us time, so governments should start **training funds** now.
Banking jobs will look **different** by 2031, so learn more than paper processing.
think: It's a **ticking clock** I can work with, and by 27 I could have a promotion.
The risk is staying in the back office and doing the **same thing** for four years.
do: Move to **underwriting or advice** in two years and get a recognised qualification.
Consider a **smaller firm** and put 100 a month on the loan.
feel: **Okay**, like seeing a storm on the forecast and buying a coat.
S3.quote: In the big bank I'm one of eighty people doing one step. In a small firm I'd see the whole process and be harder to replace.
fieldNote: Sees **breadth** as protection, a considered, centrist plan.
Would stay for a **written plan** from the bank, not vague promises.
Remains anxious because the **pay risk** is still real.

steps.text: Transfer to the underwriting team within two years
Earn a recognised credit analyst qualification at weekends
Save 100 a month and pay the loan down early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan. I'd back retraining schemes and a reasonable tax on gains, and I'd tell friends not to freak out. I'd say it with a straight face even if I wasn't sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for me. I'd be 32 and could have a mortgage, a decent role and maybe a family. The possible downside is that I coast along because it's not urgent, and wake up in 2035 with a job that's gone and no new skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first three years to get qualified and cleared of most of my loan. Then I'd decide whether to stay in banking, move to the regulator's side, or go into something like compliance, where rules and people matter. I'd learn the AI tools at the same pace as everybody else. And I'd buy a small flat with Emre or alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's the sort of picture where I can still have a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal life look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat I own, maybe two kids, holidays I don't feel guilty about. I'd like to help my parents with their roof. That's all. I don't need a big dream, just steady footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop yourself from coasting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set goals every year and tell Emre so he can nag me. And keep a rule: every two years I have to learn something new, even if the job doesn't demand it.

say: Ten years is enough to **plan**, and I'd back retraining schemes.
I'd tell friends **not to freak out**, even if I'm not sure.
think: For me it's **good news**: at 32 I could have a mortgage and a decent role.
The downside is **coasting** because it isn't urgent.
do: Spend three years getting **qualified** and clearing most of the loan.
Then pick between **compliance**, the regulator's side or staying in banking.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with a normal life still in view.
S4.quote: I'd like to help my parents with their roof. That's all. I don't need a big dream, just steady footing.
fieldNote: Wants **steady footing**, not a big dream, which matches his centrist outlook.
Plans a rule of learning something new every **two years**.
Mood eases to uneasy: **income** looks safe, but the world around him is changing.

steps.text: Qualify as a credit analyst and clear most of the loan by 2029
Save a deposit for a one-bedroom flat
Help my parents pay for their roof repair
Learn each new AI tool the bank brings in

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no savings and a loan. What would help is a clear plan in writing from the bank, support for retraining on paid time and a fair way to move into other work. I'd also like the government to say what happens to the loan if the jobs go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that my brother and I are the same people on different tracks. If one of us can help the other, we'll be fine. I don't think the economy knows that.

headlineQuote: My brother and I are the same people on different tracks. If one of us can help the other, we'll be fine.
portrait: Erik is a **22-year-old** loan processing clerk at a regional bank, sharing a flat with his brother Emre.
He uses AI now and then, adopts tools **once they're proven** and treats them as practical.
He is centrist, wants **written plans** and fair retraining rather than slogans.
His exposure is plain: document checking and number entry are the first tasks software takes.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years, easing again with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no savings, a loan and a job at the front of the cuts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written plan** from the bank, paid retraining time and clear government word on what happens to student loans.
